## What it says
A topologically finitely generated profinite group is determined, up to topological isomorphism, by its continuous finite quotients.

- `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is a profinite group, a compact, totally disconnected topological group.
- `[Group H] [TopologicalSpace H] [IsTopologicalGroup H] [CompactSpace H] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace H]`: $H$ is a profinite group too.
- `(hG : IsTopologicallyFinitelyGenerated G)`: some finite subset of $G$ generates a dense subgroup.
- `(h : ∀ (Q : Type u) [inst : Group Q] [Finite Q], IsFiniteContinuousQuotient G Q ↔ IsFiniteContinuousQuotient H Q)`: for every finite group $Q$, some surjective homomorphism $G \to Q$ has open kernel exactly when some $H \to Q$ does.
- The conclusion, `Nonempty (G ≃ₜ* H)`: some group isomorphism $G \to H$ is also a homeomorphism.

This is the classical theorem in its sharp form: finite generation is asked of $G$ alone, and for $H$ it follows from the hypotheses.

## References and tests
- ProfiniteProPGroups, `Completed/ProfiniteProPGroups/README.md`, The isomorphism theorem, sharp form: the TauCetiRoadmap target this theorem fills.
- Ribes–Zalesskii Thm. 3.2.9 — the source the roadmap gives for the theorem.
- Fried–Jarden — the roadmap's other source.
- Dixon–Formanek–Poland–Ribes 1982 — to whom Voyager's announcement attributes the result.
- `TauCeti.exists_surjective_and_exists_surjective_of_forall_isFiniteContinuousQuotient_iff` — passes: under the same hypotheses there are continuous surjective homomorphisms $G \to H$ and $H \to G$.
- `TauCeti.IsTopologicallyFinitelyGenerated.of_forall_isFiniteContinuousQuotient` — passes: a profinite $H$ each of whose continuous finite quotients is one of a topologically finitely generated $G$ is itself topologically finitely generated, which is why $H$ needs no such hypothesis.
- `TauCeti.isFiniteContinuousQuotient_iff_exists_continuous` — passes: for a finite discrete group $Q$, a surjection with open kernel is the same as a continuous surjection, so these are the usual continuous quotients.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsFiniteContinuousQuotient G Q` asks for an open kernel rather than continuity into a topology on $Q$; the last test shows the two agree for discrete $Q$.
- $Q$ ranges over finite groups in the universe `u` of $G$ and $H$, a level of Lean's hierarchy of types. Every finite group has an isomorphic copy there, and the roadmap records that the predicate depends only on $Q$ up to isomorphism, so all finite groups count.
- `≃ₜ*` is a group isomorphism that is also a homeomorphism; `Nonempty` asserts that one exists, without singling one out.
- Profiniteness is carried by typeclasses, hypotheses in square brackets that Lean finds by itself.

## What it says
Serre's theorem at arbitrary rank: a pro-$p$ group $G$ with $\mathrm{cd}_p G \le 1$ is free pro-$p$ on generators converging to $1$, with no finite generation assumed.

- `[Fact (Nat.Prime p)]`: the natural number $p$ is prime.
- `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is a compact, totally disconnected topological group, that is, a profinite group.
- `(hG : IsProP p G)`: $G$ is pro-$p$: its quotient by each open normal subgroup is a $p$-group.
- `(hcd : cohomologicalDimensionAt p G ≤ 1)`: the $p$-cohomological dimension of $G$ is at most $1$.
- The conclusion: some subset $s \subseteq G$ converges to $1$ (each neighbourhood of $1$ holds all but finitely many of its elements), and some topological group isomorphism $e$ from `freeProPInsertOne p s`, the free pro-$p$ group on the pointed space $(s \cup \{1\}, 1)$, onto $G$ has as its underlying map the presentation `hG.presentation s`, which sends each generator to itself in $G$.

So $s$ is a basis of $G$ converging to $1$: $G$ is free pro-$p$ in the classical sense, of arbitrary rank, and the isomorphism is the one the generators induce.

## References and tests
- ProfiniteProPGroups, `Completed/ProfiniteProPGroups/README.md`, Layer 10, Serre's theorem in full generality: the roadmap target this theorem fills.
- Ribes–Zalesskii Cor. 7.7.5 — the source the roadmap gives.
- Serre, Galois Cohomology I §4.2 — which Voyager's announcement of this theorem cites for the vanishing of cohomology on free pro-$p$ groups.
- `TauCeti.IsProP.nonempty_continuousMulEquiv_freeProP_of_cohomologicalDimensionAt_le_one` — passes: a topologically finitely generated such $G$ is free pro-$p$ on a finite set whose size is its least number of topological generators.
- `TauCeti.freeProP.cohomologicalDimensionAt_le_one` — passes: free pro-$p$ groups have $\mathrm{cd}_p \le 1$, so real groups meet the hypothesis.
- `TauCeti.IsProP.presentation_of` — passes: the presentation sends each generator to its point of $G$.
- `TauCeti.IsProP.exists_convergesToOne_presentation_surjective_ker_le_proPFrattini` — passes: every pro-$p$ group has a surjective presentation on a set converging to $1$, with kernel in the Frattini subgroup.
- `TauCeti.isProjective_freeProCPointed` — passes: a free pro-$p$ group on a pointed space is projective.

## Lean subtleties
- Bracketed hypotheses are typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. Compactness and total disconnectedness make $G$ profinite; `IsProP` alone would not.
- `≃ₜ*` is a group isomorphism that is a homeomorphism; `⇑e = ⇑(hG.presentation s)` makes it the presentation itself, not some other isomorphism.
- The free object is free on a pointed space: its homomorphisms correspond to continuous maps on $s \cup \{1\}$ sending $1$ to $1$. Convergence to $1$ puts no bound on the size of $s$.
- `cohomologicalDimensionAt` takes values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots, \infty\}$, with $\infty$ when no bound exists. For the trivial group, $s$ may be empty.

## What it says
The free profinite group on a set $X$: the profinite completion of the free group on $X$.

- `(X : Type u)`: the set of generators, any type, finite or infinite.
- The type: an object of `ProfiniteGrp`, the category of profinite groups (compact, totally disconnected topological groups), in the universe of $X$.

Its value is `ProfiniteGrp.ProfiniteCompletion.completion` of the free group `FreeGroup X`, made an object of the category of groups by `GrpCat.of`: the inverse limit $\varprojlim F(X)/N$ of the quotients of the abstract free group $F(X)$ by its normal subgroups $N$ of finite index. This is the free profinite group on $X$ as a discrete set: every map from $X$ to a profinite group extends uniquely to a continuous homomorphism, since every homomorphism from $F(X)$ to a finite group has a kernel of finite index. That universal property characterises the free profinite group in the literature, and the tests prove it for this construction.

## References and tests
- Ribes–Zalesskii Ch. 3 — free profinite groups and their universal property, as Voyager's announcement cites it.
- ProfiniteProPGroups, `Completed/ProfiniteProPGroups/README.md`, Layer 4, Construction of the free objects: defines the free profinite group as the profinite completion of the free group, with its generators and universal property.
- `TauCeti.freeProfiniteGroup.existsUnique_lift` — passes: every map $f$ from $X$ to a compact, totally disconnected topological group $P$ in the same universe extends uniquely to a continuous homomorphism $\varphi$ with $\varphi(x) = f(x)$ on generators.
- `TauCeti.freeProfiniteGroup.existsUnique_continuousMulEquiv` — passes: any such group $G$ with a map $\iota : X \to G$ having the same universal property is isomorphic to it as a topological group, by a unique isomorphism matching the generators.
- `TauCeti.freeProfiniteGroup.map_surjective` — passes: a surjection $X \to Y$ induces a surjective continuous homomorphism of free profinite groups.

The first two tests are the universal property and the uniqueness up to unique isomorphism that define the free profinite group, so this construction is that object and not merely some completion.

## Lean subtleties
- It is an `abbrev`, so Lean unfolds it to the completion wherever needed.
- `ProfiniteGrp.{u}` bundles a profinite group with its topology, in universe `u`, a level of Lean's hierarchy of types; the universal property in the tests is for target groups in the same universe as $X$, which does not limit the mathematics.
- For an infinite $X$ this is the free profinite group on $X$ as a discrete set, with no condition on the generators; it is a different object from the free profinite group on a set converging to $1$.
- For the empty type $X$ the free group is trivial, and so is its completion.

## What it says
For an extension $L/K$ of nonarchimedean local fields with compatible valuations, the proposition that $L/K$ is unramified: $e(L/K) = 1$ and the residue field extension is separable.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$ is a nonarchimedean local field: a locally compact field whose topology comes from an equivalence class of nontrivial valuations, such as a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ or of $\mathbb{F}_q((t))$.
- `[Field L] [ValuativeRel L] [TopologicalSpace L] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField L]`: $L$ is one too.
- `[Algebra K L] [ValuativeExtension K L]`: $L$ is an extension of $K$ whose valuation induces that of $K$.

It is a class with two fields:

- `ramificationIndex_eq_one`: $e(L/K) = 1$, where $e(L/K)$ is the index of the image of $K^\times$ in the value group of the normalised valuation of $L$.
- `isSeparable_residueField`: the residue field of $L$ is separable over that of $K$.

This is the standard notion for extensions of discretely valued fields. Residue fields of local fields are finite, hence perfect, so the second field is automatic here; the docstring keeps it because it belongs to the general notion.

## References and tests
- Serre, *Corps Locaux* I §4, III §5: the ramification index, and unramified extensions.
- LocalFieldsRamification, `Completed/LocalFieldsRamification/README.md`, Layer 2, The arithmetic predicate: the map of value groups is bijective, that is $e(L/K) = 1$, and the residue extension is separable.
- `TauCeti.isUnramified_iff_formallyUnramified` — $L/K$ is unramified exactly when the ring of integers of $L$ is formally unramified over that of $K$, Mathlib's algebraic notion.
- `TauCeti.isUnramified_tower_iff` — for $K \subseteq L \subseteq M$, $M/K$ is unramified exactly when $L/K$ and $M/L$ both are.
- `TauCeti.DyadicSqrtTwo.not_isUnramified` — $\mathbb{Q}_2(\sqrt{2})/\mathbb{Q}_2$ is not unramified.
- `TauCeti.DyadicSqrtFive.inertiaDegree_eq_two` — $\mathbb{Q}_2(\sqrt{5})$, the unramified quadratic example, has residue degree $2$ over $\mathbb{Q}_2$.

All four pass. They tie the class to the étale notion, give the classical behaviour in towers, and separate a ramified quadratic extension from an unramified one.

## Lean subtleties
- Every hypothesis is a typeclass, found by Lean itself. `ValuativeRel` records an equivalence class of valuations; the normalised valuation is derived from it.
- No finiteness of $L/K$ is assumed: a local field over a local field, with compatible valuations, is a finite extension, being a locally compact vector space over it.
- The ramification index is a natural number, the index of a subgroup; Mathlib gives an infinite index the value $0$, which the condition $= 1$ excludes anyway.
- $L = K$ is unramified, and no Galois hypothesis is part of the notion.

## What it says
Dedekind's theorem in Frobenius form, with the fixed points counted separately.

- `[Field M] [NumberField M]`: $M$ is a number field.
- `[Fact (Nat.Prime p)]`: $p$ is prime.
- `[Field K] [NumberField K]`: $K$ is a number field, and $\theta$ lies in its ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$.
- `(hsq : Squarefree (Polynomial.map (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) (minpoly ℤ θ)))`: $f$ = `minpoly ℤ θ`, the monic minimal polynomial of $\theta$ over $\mathbb{Z}$, is squarefree modulo $p$.
- `[Fact (Polynomial.map (algebraMap ℚ M) (minpoly ℚ ↑θ)).Splits]`: $f$ splits into linear factors over $M$.
- `(Q : Ideal (NumberField.RingOfIntegers M))`: an ideal $Q$ of $\mathcal{O}_M$.
- `[Q.IsPrime] [Q.LiesOver (Ideal.span {↑p})]`: $Q$ is prime and lies over $p$.
- `(hσ : IsArithFrobAt ℤ σ Q)`: $\sigma$, an automorphism of $M$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, is an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$: $\sigma(x) \equiv x^p \pmod Q$ on $\mathcal{O}_M$.
- The conclusion: the degrees of the distinct monic irreducible factors of $f \bmod p$ form the cycle type of the permutation $\sigma$ induces on the roots of $f$ in $M$, plus one part $1$ per fixed root.

The roadmap target also assumes $p \nmid$ `RingOfIntegers.exponent θ`, $K = \mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ and $M$ Galois; squarefreeness alone suffices, since reduction modulo $Q$ then matches the roots of $f$ bijectively with those of $f \bmod p$, carrying $\sigma$ to $x \mapsto x^p$.

## References and tests
- NumberFieldArithmetic, `Completed/NumberFieldArithmetic/README.md`, 3.9 Dedekind's theorem: the target, under the name suggested there, with the fixed points added as it prescribes.
- Neukirch I §8 Exercises 4 and 5 — the roadmap's source.
- Marcus Ch. 4 — the roadmap's other source.

Four tests are recorded, all passing; they check the two sides on cases known by hand:

- `Polynomial.factorDegrees_X_pow_five_sub_X_sub_one_two` — $X^5 - X - 1$ factors modulo $2$ with degrees $3$ and $2$.
- `Polynomial.factorDegrees_X_pow_five_sub_X_sub_one_five` — modulo $5$ it is irreducible.
- `Polynomial.not_squarefree_map_X_pow_three_add_X_sq_sub_two_mul_X_add_eight_zmod_two` — $X^3 + X^2 - 2X + 8$, the roadmap's Dedekind cubic with $X$ replaced by $-X$, is not squarefree modulo $2$: `hsq` excludes the case where unramifiedness alone would mislead.
- `Equiv.Perm.fullCycleType_one` — the identity's full cycle type is all $1$s, fixed points counting as parts $1$, as on the right side here.

## Lean subtleties
- Mathlib's `cycleType` omits cycles of length $1$; the summand `Multiset.replicate (Nat.card …) 1` restores them, so the right side is a partition of $\deg f$. `monicFactorsMod θ p` is a finite set listing each factor once; under `hsq` none repeats.
- `minpoly ℚ ↑θ` is `minpoly ℤ θ` read over $\mathbb{Q}$, as $\theta$ is integral; `↑θ` is $\theta$ viewed in $K$.
- For monic $f$, `hsq` is equivalent to the classical $p \nmid \operatorname{disc} f$.
- `Gal(M/ℚ)` is the automorphism group of $M$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, Galois or not; $\sigma$ is given, and in a Galois $M$ one exists at every such $Q$.

## What it says
The structure of the multiplicative group of a nonarchimedean local field attached to a uniformizer: $K^\times \cong \mathbb{Z} \times \mathcal{O}_K^\times$ as topological groups.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$ is a nonarchimedean local field: a locally compact field whose topology comes from a nontrivial valuation, given up to equivalence.
- `(ϖ : Kˣ)`: a nonzero element $\varpi$ of $K$.
- `(hϖ : (normalizedValuation K) ϖ = Multiplicative.ofAdd 1)`: the normalized valuation $v_K$, with values in $\mathbb{Z}$, is $1$ at $\varpi$: $\varpi$ is a uniformizer.

The value is an isomorphism of topological groups from $K^\times$ to $\mathbb{Z} \times U(K, 0)$, where $U(K, 0)$ = `unitFiltration K 0` is the unit group $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ of the valuation ring. It sends $x$ to $(v_K(x),\ x\varpi^{-v_K(x)})$; its inverse sends $(n, u)$ to $\varpi^n u$; both maps are continuous.

This is the standard splitting $K^\times = \varpi^{\mathbb{Z}} \times \mathcal{O}_K^\times$, made topological. It depends on $\varpi$, as in the literature, and covers equal and mixed characteristic alike.

## References and tests
- Serre, *Corps Locaux*, II §§4–5 — the multiplicative group of a local field, as Voyager's announcement cites it.
- Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, II.5.3 — the decomposition of $K^\times$, also cited there.
- LocalFieldsRamification, `Completed/LocalFieldsRamification/README.md`, Layer 1, Structure of `Kˣ`: asks for this topological isomorphism attached to a choice of uniformizer, and names this definition for it.
- `TauCeti.normalizedValuation_comp_zpowersHom` — passes: $v_K(\varpi^n) = n$ for every integer $n$, so $n \mapsto \varpi^n$ splits the valuation.
- `TauCeti.existsUnique_eq_zpow_mul` — passes: every $x \in K^\times$ is $\varpi^n u$ for exactly one $(n, u) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathcal{O}_K^\times$, negative $n$ included.
- `TauCeti.unitsEquivIntProd_trans_prodShear` — passes: for another uniformizer $\varpi'$, the isomorphism for $\varpi'$ is the one for $\varpi$ followed by the shear $(n, u) \mapsto (n, (\varpi/\varpi')^n u)$.

The first two give the bijection behind the isomorphism; the third pins down how it depends on the uniformizer.

## Lean subtleties
- `≃ₜ*` is a group isomorphism that is also a homeomorphism.
- `Multiplicative ℤ` is $\mathbb{Z}$ written multiplicatively, with the discrete topology; `Multiplicative.ofAdd 1` is the integer $1$ there.
- `unitFiltration K 0` asks for units congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak{m}^0 = \mathcal{O}_K$, which every unit is: it is all of $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$, not the principal units $1 + \mathfrak{m}$.
- Negative powers of $\varpi$ are taken in the group $K^\times$, so no division by zero occurs.

## What it says
The smooth local geodesic flow of a Riemannian manifold.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real normed space, the model vector space.
- `[TopologicalSpace H]`: $H$ is the model space, and $I$ a model with corners from $H$ to $E$.
- `[TopologicalSpace M] [ChartedSpace H M] [I.Boundaryless] [IsManifold I (↑⊤) M]`: $M$ is a smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on $I$.
- `[Bundle.RiemannianBundle fun (x : M) => TangentSpace I x] [IsContMDiffRiemannianBundle I (↑⊤) E fun (x : M) => TangentSpace I x]`: $M$ carries a smooth Riemannian metric.
- `(z : TangentBundle I M)`: a point $z$ of the tangent bundle $TM$.
- The conclusion: there are a neighbourhood $U$ of $z$ in $TM$, an open neighbourhood $s$ of $0$ in $\mathbb{R}$, and a map $\Phi : TM \times \mathbb{R} \to TM$, jointly $C^\infty$ at $(z, 0)$, such that for every $w \in U$: $\Phi(w, 0) = w$; $t \mapsto \Phi(w, t)$ is an integral curve on $s$ of the geodesic spray $(x, v) \mapsto (v, -\Gamma_x(v, v))$; $\Phi(w, t + u) = \Phi(\Phi(w, t), u)$ for $t \in s$ and all real $u$; and the projection of $t \mapsto \Phi(w, t)$ to $M$ is a geodesic on $s$ with the position (`w.proj`) and velocity (`w.snd`) that $w$ encodes.

Geodesics are the projections of the spray's integral curves, and this is their local existence with smooth dependence on initial data, asserted at $(z, 0)$.

## References and tests
- Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Thm 9.12 — the fundamental theorem on flows, as Voyager's announcement cites it.
- do Carmo, *Riemannian Geometry*, Ch. 3 §2 — the geodesic flow, also cited there.
- HopfRinow, `Completed/HopfRinow/README.md`, Layer 1, Smooth dependence and the local geodesic flow: the milestone that takes from this theorem its common neighbourhoods and smooth local spray trajectories.
- `TauCeti.Manifold.exists_contMDiffAt_localFlow` — passes: the same local flow for any smooth vector field on a finite-dimensional manifold without boundary; for the spray on $TM$ it gives every clause here but the last.
- `IsMIntegralCurveOn.isGeodesicCurveOnFrom_proj` — passes: an integral curve of the spray through $w$ at time $0$, on a set containing $0$ with unique derivatives, projects to a geodesic with the position and velocity of $w$, so the velocity is genuinely constrained.

## Lean subtleties
- `(↑⊤)` is the smoothness level $\infty$: $C^\infty$, not analytic.
- `ContMDiffAt` at the point $(z, 0)$ means, in Mathlib, $C^k$ near it for every finite $k$; smoothness on a whole flow domain is a separate result.
- $\Phi$ is a total map: only its values for $w \in U$ and $t \in s$ are the flow, the rest constrained only by the flow law.
- Neither completeness nor Hausdorffness is assumed; a zero vector gives the constant geodesic.

## What it says
Burnside's basis theorem for pro-$p$ groups, generation form: a subset topologically generates a pro-$p$ group exactly when its image topologically generates the Frattini quotient.

- `[hp : Fact (Nat.Prime p)]`: $p$ is a prime number.
- `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is a compact, totally disconnected topological group, that is, a profinite group.
- `(hG : IsProP p G)`: $G$ is pro-$p$: its quotient by every open normal subgroup is a $p$-group.
- `(s : Set G)`: any subset $s$ of $G$.
- The conclusion: the closure of the subgroup generated by $s$ is all of $G$ if and only if the same holds for the image of $s$ in $G/\Phi_p(G)$, where $\Phi_p(G)$ = `proPFrattini p G` is the intersection of the open normal subgroups of index $p$, and `QuotientGroup.mk'` is the quotient map.

This is the standard Burnside basis theorem for pro-$p$ groups, with topological generation on both sides and no finite-generation hypothesis.

## References and tests
- Ribes–Zalesskii, §2.8 — the Frattini subgroup of a pro-$p$ group and Burnside's basis theorem, as Voyager's announcement cites it.
- Ribes–Zalesskii Prop. 2.8.7 and §2.8 — the source the roadmap gives.
- ProfiniteProPGroups, `Completed/ProfiniteProPGroups/README.md`, Layer 3, Burnside basis theorem: a subset generates $G$ topologically if and only if its image generates $G/\Phi(G)$ topologically, with the closure kept on the quotient side; this theorem is listed as its implementation.
- `TauCeti.IsProP.eq_top_of_sup_proPFrattini_eq_top` — passes: a closed subgroup $H$ with $H\Phi_p(G) = G$ is all of $G$, so $\Phi_p(G)$ consists of non-generators, the heart of the converse.
- `TauCeti.IsProP.eq_top_of_forall_not_le_openNormalSubgroup_index_eq` — passes: a closed subgroup contained in no open normal subgroup of index $p$ is all of $G$, with no finite-generation hypothesis.

## Lean subtleties
- `Subgroup.closure s` is the abstract subgroup generated by $s$, and `topologicalClosure` its closure. Both are needed: at infinite rank the image of a generating set may span only a dense subgroup of $G/\Phi_p(G)$.
- `proPFrattini p G` is the Frattini subgroup of the profinite theory, which can differ from the abstract Frattini subgroup when $G$ is not finitely generated. It is closed and normal, so $G/\Phi_p(G)$, with the quotient topology, is again a topological group.
- For $s = \varnothing$ both sides say that $G$ is trivial: a nontrivial pro-$p$ group has $\Phi_p(G) \neq G$.

## What it says
For a Henselian local ring $R$ whose residue field $k$ is finite, of order $q$, the Teichmüller lift on units: the group homomorphism $\omega : k^\times \to R^\times$ sending each $x$ to the unique $(q-1)$-st root of unity of $R$ that reduces to $x$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with a $1$.
- `[HenselianLocalRing R]`: $R$ is a local ring in which simple roots over the residue field of polynomials over $R$ lift to roots in $R$ (Hensel's lemma).
- `[Finite (IsLocalRing.ResidueField R)]`: the residue field $k$, the quotient of $R$ by its maximal ideal, is finite.
- The type `(IsLocalRing.ResidueField R)ˣ →* Rˣ`: a homomorphism from the unit group $k^\times$ to the unit group $R^\times$.

Its value: `rootsOfUnityMulEquivUnitsResidueField R`, the isomorphism by reduction from the group $\mu_{q-1}(R)$ of $(q-1)$-st roots of unity of $R$ onto $k^\times$, with $q$ = `Nat.card (ResidueField R)`, inverted and followed by the inclusion of $\mu_{q-1}(R)$ in $R^\times$. So $\omega(x)$ reduces to $x$ and $\omega(x)^{q-1} = 1$.

This is the classical Teichmüller representative, stated for every Henselian local ring with finite residue field, the ring of integers of a nonarchimedean local field among them.

## References and tests
- Serre, *Corps Locaux*, II §4 — the Teichmüller section, as Voyager's announcement cites it.
- LocalFieldsRamification, `Completed/LocalFieldsRamification/README.md`, Layer 1, Teichmüller: the multiplicative section of reduction, characterized as the unique one with values in the $(q-1)$-torsion.

Six tests are recorded, all passing; they compute the lift where it is known by hand:

- `TauCeti.Padic.teichmuller_padic_two` — over the integers of $\mathbb Q_2$, whose residue field $\mathbb F_2$ has trivial unit group, the lift is the constant homomorphism $1$.
- `TauCeti.coe_teichmuller_apply` — for a nonarchimedean local field, the lift agrees on units with the zero-preserving Teichmüller lift, which the remaining tests compute.
- `TauCeti.Padic.teichmullerLift_padic_five_four` — in $\mathbb Q_5$ the lift of $4 = -1$ is $-1$.
- `TauCeti.Padic.teichmullerLift_padic_five_two_sq` — in $\mathbb Q_5$ the lift of $2$ squares to $-1$.
- `TauCeti.Padic.isPrimitiveRoot_teichmullerLift_padic_five_two` — it is a primitive fourth root of unity, as $2$ has order $4$ in $\mathbb F_5^\times$.
- `TauCeti.Padic.teichmullerLift_padic_five_three` — the lift of $3 = -2$ is minus the lift of $2$.

## Lean subtleties
- The three bracketed hypotheses are typeclasses, found by Lean itself; `HenselianLocalRing` includes that $R$ is local.
- $q$ is `Nat.card` of the residue field, its number of elements, which would be $0$ for an infinite type, as `Finite` rules out. `Nat.card … - 1` is subtraction on ℕ, stopping at $0$, but a field has at least two elements, so $q - 1 \geq 1$.
- $R$ need not be a domain or complete, and the lift is defined on $k^\times$ only.

## What it says
The verbal description of the pro-$p$ Frattini subgroup: for a profinite group $G$ and a prime $p$, the intersection $\Phi_p(G)$ of the open normal subgroups of index $p$ is $\overline{G^p[G,G]}$, the closure of the subgroup generated by the $p$-th powers and the commutators.

- `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G]`: $G$ is a topological group.
- `[CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]`: $G$ is compact and totally disconnected; together, $G$ is a profinite group.

## What it says
The Schwarz reflection principle across the real axis: on an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ symmetric under conjugation, the reflection of a function $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ that is continuous on the closed upper part of $\Omega$, holomorphic on its open upper part and real at its real points, is holomorphic on $\Omega$.

- `(hΩopen : IsOpen Ω)`: $\Omega$ is open.
- `(hΩ : Set.MapsTo (⇑(starRingEnd ℂ)) Ω Ω)`: complex conjugation maps $\Omega$ into itself; as conjugation is an involution, $\overline{\Omega} = \Omega$.
- `(hcont : ContinuousOn f (Ω ∩ {z : ℂ | 0 ≤ z.im}))`: $f$ is continuous on $\Omega \cap \{\operatorname{Im} z \ge 0\}$.
- `(hholo : DifferentiableOn ℂ f (Ω ∩ {z : ℂ | 0 < z.im}))`: $f$ is complex differentiable at each point of the open set $\Omega \cap \{\operatorname{Im} z > 0\}$, so holomorphic there.
- `(hreal : ∀ z ∈ Ω, z.im = 0 → (f z).im = 0)`: $f$ is real at every real point of $\Omega$.
- The conclusion: `schwarzReflection f`, equal to $f(z)$ when $\operatorname{Im} z \ge 0$ and to $\overline{f(\bar z)}$ when $\operatorname{Im} z < 0$, is complex differentiable at each point of $\Omega$, so holomorphic on the open set $\Omega$.

This is the classical reflection principle in its common elementary form, with $f$ itself continuous up to the axis; forms built on harmonic functions assume only that $\operatorname{Im} f$ extends continuously by $0$ to the axis. No connectedness of $\Omega$ is needed, since the gluing is local.

## What it says
The generalized winding number of a curve $\gamma$ on $[a, b]$ about a point $z_0$, which may lie on the curve:
$$n_{z_0}(\gamma) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\, \mathrm{PV}\!\oint_\gamma \frac{dz}{z - z_0}.$$

- `(γ : ℝ → ℂ)`: a curve, a map from the reals to the complex plane, taken on the parameter interval from $a$ to $b$.
- `(a b : ℝ)`: the ends of that interval.
- `(z₀ : ℂ)`: the point, on or off the curve.
- The value: $(2\pi i)^{-1}$ times `cauchyPVAt γ a b (fun z => (z - z₀)⁻¹) z₀`, the Cauchy principal value of $\oint_\gamma dz/(z - z_0)$: the limit, as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$, of the integral over the part of the curve outside the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about $z_0$.

This is the generalized winding number of Hungerbühler and Wasem. For a continuous curve that avoids $z_0$, nothing is cut out once $\varepsilon$ is small, and it is the classical index $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{dz}{z - z_0}$; at a point of the curve it may be fractional, such as $1/2$ at a smooth point.

## What it says
The homology form of Cauchy's theorem: if $f$ is holomorphic on an open set $\Omega$, and $\gamma$ is a closed piecewise $C^1$ curve in $\Omega$ whose winding number about every point outside $\Omega$ is $0$, then $\oint_\gamma f(z)\, dz = 0$.

- `(hΩ : IsOpen Ω)`: $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is open.
- `(γ : ℝ → ℂ)`: a curve $\gamma$, a map from the reals to the complex plane.
- `(a b : ℝ)`: the ends of the parameter interval on which $\gamma$ is used.
- `(hγ_pc1 : IsPiecewiseC1On γ a b)`: $\gamma$ is piecewise $C^1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $b$: continuous there, and differentiable off finitely many breakpoints with an integrable derivative; corners are allowed.
- `(hγ : ∀ t ∈ Set.uIcc a b, γ t ∈ Ω)`: the curve lies in $\Omega$.
- `(hclosed : γ a = γ b)`: the curve is closed.
- `(hf : DifferentiableOn ℂ f Ω)`: $f$ is complex differentiable at every point of the open set $\Omega$, that is, holomorphic there.
- `(hnull : IsNullHomologous γ a b Ω)`: $\gamma$ is null-homologous in $\Omega$: its generalized winding number about every point outside $\Omega$ is $0$.
- The conclusion: $\int_a^b \gamma'(t)\, f(\gamma(t))\, dt = 0$, which is the contour integral $\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz$.

This is the general homology version of Cauchy's theorem, stated for one closed curve rather than a cycle. It does not ask $\Omega$ to be simply connected: $\Omega$ may have holes, so long as $\gamma$ does not wind around them.

## What it says
An elliptic curve $E$ over a field $F$ has geometric complex multiplication when some endomorphism of $E$ over a separable closure of $F$ is not multiplication by an integer.

- `(W : WeierstrassCurve F)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $F$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is a unit of $F$, that is nonzero, so $W$ is an elliptic curve $E$.

This is the usual definition: $E$ has complex multiplication when its geometric endomorphism ring is larger than $\mathbb{Z}$, as the docstring says. In characteristic $0$ that ring is then an order in an imaginary quadratic field; in positive characteristic it may also be an order in a quaternion algebra, and the definition keeps the same meaning, a ring larger than $\mathbb{Z}$.

## What it says
The conductor of an elliptic curve over the fraction field $K$ of a Dedekind domain $O$, as the ideal $\prod_v \mathfrak{p}_v^{f_v}$ of $O$, with each exponent $f_v$ read off Tate's algorithm through Ogg's formula.

- `[CommRing O] [IsDedekindDomain O]`: $O$ is a Dedekind domain, such as the ring of integers of a number field.
- `[∀ (v : IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum O), PerfectField (IsLocalRing.ResidueField (Localization.AtPrime v.asIdeal))]`: at every nonzero prime $v$ of $O$, the residue field of the localisation $O_v$ is perfect, as Tate's algorithm requires; finite residue fields, as for number fields, are perfect.
- `[Field K] [Algebra O K] [IsFractionRing O K]`: $K$ is the fraction field of $O$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is nonzero, so $W$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: the product, over the nonzero primes $v$ of $O$ with $f_v \neq 0$, of the ideals $\mathfrak{p}_v^{f_v}$, where $f_v$ is `W.algorithmicOggExponent (Localization.AtPrime v.asIdeal)`, the algorithmic Ogg exponent $f_v = v(\Delta_{\min,v}) - m_v + 1$: here $v(\Delta_{\min,v})$ is the valuation of the discriminant of a minimal equation at $v$, and $m_v$ the number of components of the Kodaira symbol of the reduction that Tate's algorithm finds.

By Ogg's formula, $v(\Delta_{\min,v}) = f_v + m_v - 1$, where $f_v$ is the exponent of the conductor at $v$; so this ideal is the conductor of the curve. Good reduction gives $f_v = 0$ and multiplicative reduction $f_v = 1$.

## What it says
Siegel's lemma in Bombieri and Vaaler's form: $p$ independent linear equations with integer coefficients in $n > p$ unknowns have a nonzero integer solution $x$ with $\max_i |x_i| \le \bigl(\sqrt{\det(AA^{T})}/g\bigr)^{1/(n-p)}$, where $g$ is the gcd of the maximal minors of the coefficient matrix $A$.

- `[Fintype ι]`: the type $\iota$ indexing the unknowns is finite, and $n$ = `Fintype.card ι` is its number of elements. The matrix $A$, an implicit argument, is a $p \times n$ integer matrix, its rows indexed by `Fin p`, the numbers $0, \dots, p-1$, and its columns by $\iota$.
- `(hA : LinearIndependent ℚ (A.map Int.cast).row)`: the rows of $A$, read as vectors with rational entries, are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, so $A$ has rank $p$.
- `(hp : p < Fintype.card ι)`: fewer equations than unknowns, $p < n$.
- The conclusion: some $x \in \mathbb{Z}^\iota$ has $x \neq 0$, $Ax = 0$ (`A.mulVec x = 0`) and $\|x\| \le (\sqrt{\det(AA^{T})}/g)^{1/(n-p)}$. Here $\|x\| = \max_i |x_i|$; $\det(AA^{T})$ is the determinant of the $p \times p$ integer matrix `A * A.transpose`; and $g$ = `A.minorGcd` is the gcd of the $p \times p$ minors of $A$; both are read as real numbers.

Bombieri and Vaaler's theorem gives $n - p$ linearly independent integer solutions whose sup norms have product at most $\sqrt{\det(AA^{T})}/g$; the smallest of them meets the bound here. This statement is that one-solution form, under the same hypotheses.

- `[CommRing A] [SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A]`: $A$ is a commutative ring with $1$, and `σ` is a type of subsets of $A$ that are additive subgroups.
- `[GradedRing 𝒜]`: the subgroups $\mathcal{A}_i$ (`𝒜 i`, $i \in \mathbb{N}$) grade $A$: $A = \bigoplus_i \mathcal{A}_i$, with $1 \in \mathcal{A}_0$ and $\mathcal{A}_i \mathcal{A}_j \subseteq \mathcal{A}_{i+j}$.
- `(s : ↑((twistingSheaf 𝒜 m).presheaf.obj (Opposite.op U)))`: a section $s \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m))$, where `twistingSheaf 𝒜 m` is $\mathcal{O}(m)$.
- `(t : ↑((twistingSheaf 𝒜 n).presheaf.obj (Opposite.op U)))`: a section $t \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(n))$.
- `(x : ↥U)`: a point $x$ of $U$, a homogeneous prime ideal of $A$.
- The conclusion: the product `((mul 𝒜 U m n) s) t` $\in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}(m+n))$ takes at $x$ the value `↑s x * ↑t x`, the product of $s(x)$ and $t(x)$ in `Localizations 𝒜 x`, the localization $A_x$ of $A$ at the prime $x$.
